1: Source states the suppression prediction (effect removed) but not Murray's reported outcome as a result; I state that the effect disappears under suppression, which is the well-established result for visually presented items. Please check.
Source says phonological store traces decay in about 2 seconds unless rehearsed; omitted as a number.
2: None; the finding and implication are both stated in the source.
3: Source says a group named Brown also published data in the late 1950s but gives no first name or year; no year used.

Source concludes decay; Keppel & Underwood (1962) is known to have argued the forgetting reflected proactive interference from earlier trials. Source does not say what their alternate explanation was; I did not name it. Please check if you want it stated.
4: Source ties the effect to sensory memory as a raw-input store; the standard textbook account (a precategorical acoustic store) is not in the source and was not added.
5: Source describes Sperling's original display as a 3 by 3 letter matrix with three tones; as commonly reported, Sperling's original used larger arrays (e.g., 3 rows of 4 letters). Not stated in the deliverable; check if needed.
'Nearly 100%' and 'about a second' are the source's wording; no other numbers used.
6: Source names no researcher or year, so none is given in v22.
Source states the result as typical; no theory is named for it in the source, only that it shows forgetting is not total loss of the item.
7: Lab states roughly 50 degrees of rotation per second; the commonly cited Shepard and Metzler rate is about 60 degrees per second. Numbers omitted from the text, so no conflict in the deliverable.
'Shepard and his colleagues' in v22 is the lab's own phrasing; only the 1971 paper is dated.
8: Lab says only that 'in some circumstances' people rate the conjunction as more likely; the text keeps that wording. Lab does not name the heuristic (representativeness) so it is not named.
Lab says conjunction 'has to be less than' either event; strictly it is less than or equal. v20 original says 'less than or equal'; teaching versions follow the lab's wording.
9: Lab credits the series of experiments to Wason and Shapiro (1971); the original selection task is usually credited to Wason (1966). Kept as the lab gives it.
Lab does not show the card faces in text; the 'D without a 3' explanation for the D card is standard logic added to explain the lab's stated answer.
10: The lab does not state its specific result. The gain-wording-to-sure-option and loss-wording-to-gamble pattern is the well-established framing finding (Tversky & Kahneman 1981 in the course materials), stated as the typical pattern, not as this lab's data. Please check.
Lab says framing effects were 'noted for centuries'; kept as given.
11: No researcher or year is given in the lab, so none is attached. The 2/3 result assumes the host knows where the prize is and always opens a non-prize door; the lab states he always does this.
Lab writes 66% and 33%; text uses two-thirds and one-third (the exact values).
12: The lab defers its findings to the debriefing, so the risk-averse-for-gains, risk-seeking-for-losses pattern is stated from well-established framing and prospect-theory results, not from the lab text. Please check against the debriefing/lecture.
13: Ages (5, 6, 7 years) are stated as group labels only because the headline contrast depends on them; no counts, times or stats are given.

The 'fluid notion of function' account is the authors' favored interpretation, not proven; the paper itself lists an 'impoverished knowledge' alternative as untested, and the sample was small (later replications are only cited as an unpublished poster, Defeyter & German, 2000).
14: Abstract says adults n = 80 but the Participants section and the Declarations note report a replacement adult sample of 83 (the first sample had two extra sound conditions); the pattern of results was reported as replicated.

The paper's own conclusion is tentative: it says phonological processing, not serial-order retention, is a precondition and that the loop-style 'interference by content' idea may have been dropped prematurely, but it did not test non-speech sounds or non-serial phonological tasks.
15: At the smallest list lengths the paper did not replicate Risko and Dunn's pattern (offloaded trials were not better, and were even worse at the smallest length); the notes teach only the main contrast at larger loads.
The failure to replicate the memory-ability link is explicitly called surprising by the authors and attributed only speculatively to sample, motivation and lack of feedback.
16: The paper frames the traditional view as reasoners being unaware ('oblivious') of the error; Kahneman and Frederick's own account allows later System 2 monitoring, and the paper itself concedes its results do not rule out substitution (a minority omitted the phrase in recall) and that many incorrect reasoners were still fully confident.
The paper raises the alternative that the confidence drop reflects a disfluency or 'feeling of rightness' signal rather than sensitivity to substitution itself, and it cannot decide between the two.
Numbers for the puzzle (5 cents, 10 cents, 90 cents) are included only to answer the bat-and-ball puzzle; no sample sizes, percentages or statistics are given.
17: The paper partly fails to confirm Fagley and Miller (1997): it finds a framing effect in both men and women, whereas F&M found it only for women; it agrees with F&M that lives elicit more risk than money.

Two original hypotheses were only partly supported (the sure default did not raise risk aversion overall); the default-source analysis was exploratory and the belief question was asked after the choice, so causal direction is unclear.
The scenarios differed in personal involvement (lives of people in another country vs one's own savings), which the authors list as a limitation of the life-vs-money comparison.
18: Chein et al. (2011) report that the age x social-context interaction on behavior did not reach statistical significance at their sample size; the claim that only adolescents took more risks rests on within-group comparisons (the neural age x context interaction was significant).

The 2013 review and the 2011 paper use age labels slightly differently across studies (an earlier alone-vs-peers experiment used late adolescents aged 18 and 19, called adolescents in the review); the notes keep to the group labels adolescents, young adults, adults without ages.

The authors acknowledge the task confounds decision making with reward anticipation, so uncertainty, distraction or motor differences cannot be fully ruled out as alternative explanations; the resistance-to-peer-influence correlation was across participants of all ages in the review's description.

1: Conrad (1964): similar-sounding items recalled worse; effect persists with silent reading
Baddeley (1986): phonological loop = phonological store + articulatory control process
Murray (1968): articulatory suppression blocks recoding; predicted to remove the effect
2: Roodenrys et al. (2002): large neighborhood words recalled better than small in immediate serial recall
Implication: memory span is not a pure measure of STM capacity
3: McGeoch (1932): critique leading researchers to favor interference over decay for ~25 years
Peterson & Peterson (1959): recall of consonant trigrams falls as the rehearsal-blocking distractor lengthens
4: Neath & Surprenant (2003): auditory presentation adds extra (sound) information, explaining the modality effect
Effect shown for heard, lip-read and mouthed lists vs silent visual
5: Sperling (1960): partial report; near-perfect for cued row when cue immediate; decay to ~4.5 items at ~1 s delay
Sensory (iconic) store lasts a few hundred ms; reporting time, not perception, limited earlier results
6: No researcher named in the source for this lab
Items mostly recalled in correct position; errors fall in adjacent positions; forgetting is not complete loss of information
7: Shepard & Metzler (1971): same-or-mirror block shapes; response time rises with rotation; constant rate; mental images much like real images; influenced theories of mental representation
8: Tversky & Kahneman (1983): probability estimates differ from objective; heuristics trade accuracy for speed; conjunction fallacy
Shafir, Smith, & Osherson (1990): descriptions of people, rated likelihood of professions/activities; conjunction rated more likely
9: Wason & Shapiro (1971): abstract vs thematic rules; experience helps thematic; abstract needs logic alone
Correct abstract cards D and 7; thematic cards borrowed car and empty gas tank
10: Kahneman & Tversky (1982): summarized framing effects; same situation, different framing changes choice
11: Monty Hall 3 Door problem (game show Let's Make A Deal): always switch ~2/3, always stay ~1/3, random ~1/2
No study or researcher year is given for this lab; Monty Hall is the show host
13: German & Defeyter (2000), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review; box task analogous to Duncker (1945) candle problem; box overturned as support/step for a toy bear to reach a shelf
Preutilization (box shown holding objects) vs no preutilization
6- and 7-year-olds slower after preutilization; 5-year-olds not slowed and faster than older groups under preutilization
Without preutilization, performance improved with age
Explanation: younger children's fluid notion of function (German & Johnson, 1997); alternative of impoverished knowledge considered unlikely but untested
Adamson (1952) cited as showing adults' effect is robust
14: Leist, Lachmann, Schlittmeier, Georgi & Klatte (accepted 2022; Memory & Cognition 2023)
Irrelevant speech effect and changing-state effect in serial recall
Verbal vs spatial items; children (third graders) and adults
Verbal: changing-state speech impaired both ages, children more than adults; steady-state hurt children only
Spatial: no disruption in either group; no habituation in verbal task

Contradicts Jones et al. (1995) functional equivalence; problem for attention-capture (Cowan, 1995) and changing-state accounts; supports similarity-based/phonological interference (Salamé & Baddeley, 1982 loop tradition)
15: Morrison & Richmond (2020), Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications; registered report; replication and extension of Risko & Dunn (2015)
Cognitive offloading defined by Risko & Gilbert (2016)
Choice (could write) vs no-choice (memory only) auditory letter memory at several set sizes
Offloading improved performance, especially at higher loads; more offloading at higher loads
Failed to replicate Risko & Dunn: no relation between memory performance and offloading; working memory capacity (new prediction) did not predict offloading frequency or benefit
Offloading is a compensatory strategy across memory ability
Costs of offloading cited: Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011); Henkel (2014)
16: Hoover & Healy (2019), Decision; bat-and-ball problem from CRT (Frederick, 2005)
Answer 5 cents; intuitive wrong answer 10 cents (subtracting $1.00 from $1.10); algebra: ball + (ball + 1.00) = 1.10
Kahneman & Frederick (2002): attribute substitution, cognitive misers (also Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)
De Neys, Rossi & Houdé (2013): incorrect reasoners less confident on standard than on control (no 'more than'): substitution sensitivity
Hoover & Healy: most incorrect reasoners recalled and recognized 'more than' even after interference; processed words but not meaning
Opinion judgments (how well others would do; after Frederick, 2005) also showed error sensitivity, correlated with confidence, less ceiling; more time goes with lower confidence
17: Giuliani, Cannito, Gigliotti, Rosa, Pietroni & Palumbo (2023; online 2022), Psychological Research
Framing effect (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981; Asian disease problem): sure option for gains, risky option for losses
Default effect: preselected option favored (e.g., Johnson & Goldstein, 2003 organ donation)
Life-or-death (Asian disease) vs financial scenarios; no default, sure default, risky default

Findings: framing effect in both scenarios; more risk taking for lives than money (consistent with Fagley & Miller, 1997); risky default raised risk taking, sure default did not raise risk aversion; framing and default additive
Beliefs about default source (most rational, experts, previous respondents/chance) moderated the effect; asked after choice, so possible post-hoc rationalization
Practical point: people can be nudged toward risk more easily than toward certainty
18: Albert, Chein & Steinberg (2013), Current Directions in Psychological Science (review): adolescents not worse at risk reasoning in lab; peer context alters risk taking; maturational gap between early-remodeling reward system and gradually maturing cognitive control
Gardner & Steinberg (2005): adolescents (and undergraduates less) took more risks with peers present in driving task; adults did not
Chein, Albert, O'Brien, Uckert & Steinberg (2011), Developmental Science: fMRI Stoplight driving game, alone vs friends watching from another room
Only adolescents took more risks when observed; not overt peer pressure
Adolescents only: more ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex activity in peer condition, tied to risky (GO) decisions
Cognitive-control (lateral prefrontal) regions less engaged in adolescents than adults but not affected by peer presence
Lower self-reported resistance to peer influence associated with larger ventral-striatum peer effect
Related: peers raise preference for immediate rewards (O'Brien et al., 2011), anonymous believed observer (Weigard et al., 2011)
